en: All who encountered Beijing died.
Those blessed by Kydyr died.
The peoples who encountered Beijing died together.
Those who came died; the khan died.
All who met the Khagan died.
Kokotoy's sole warrior son,
Bokmurun, went there and died.
Serek and Syrgak the Wolf died.
Akayar and Baichoro,
Both those giants died.
Long ago, when Akkula fell to a bullet,
My father had seen Almambet die a martyr.
My father returned from striking the Khagan,
Bereft of Khan Chubak.
“I shall destroy the Khagan,” he had said,
And had his saddle straps gathered up.
While saying his prayers in Beijing,
Through his back, ah,
My father had his lung pierced by a thrust.
Returning ill from Beijing,
My formidable father, that noble lion,
Perished from this world.
That was where he went to the next world,
Smoothing his fine mustache.
That was where he went to Judgment Day,
The place my leopard father died,
The place my dear mother suffered.
Lingering at his bedside,
My poor mother, whom I cherish,
Lost my khan father
When she was thirty-two years old.
On the hills were horses with white-marked heads,
Argymaks and fine steeds mingled.
To cry out and serve him,
I who remained behind was too young.
The place my bloodthirsty father died,
The place my mother watched over him.
Smoothing his fine mustache,
His soul drawing toward Judgment Day,
Coughing in sharp bursts,
Lifting his head from the pillow,
When he tried to rise, groaning,
Blood came gushing out.
Her wailing split the rocks;
My mother's strength failed.
Coughing with heavy thuds,
Lifting his head from the bed,
When he tried to rise, groaning,
Blood poured out by the shovelful.
Born to grief, she cried aloud.
My poor, enslaved mother's strength failed.
With the blood from my father's mouth
Twelve pits were filled.
In the places of those twelve pits
Twelve plane trees sprang up.
When my leopard father passed away,
His bright eyes closed.
When my father slipped away,
“My bloodthirsty one, take me with you!”
My khan father's forty nobles
Stood in a row, sobbing.
“My bloodthirsty one, take me away!”
All leaning on their spears,
They cried aloud and wailed.
Where the forty companions stood wailing,
Groves and willows grew like an enclosure.
In this way my father
Was aided by the holy khwajas.
My lion father who went to the next world
Twisted and straightened his mustache.
None who defied my father prospered.
The prophets supported your father.
My khan father twisted and straightened his beard.
The Prophet's Companions aided my father.
When his soul departed,
That was the place they laid my father in the earth.
Groves and willows grew in clumps.
My leopard father, my lion—
In this way God came to his aid.
All the saints gathered together.
Where they washed that blessed one,
Plane trees and willows grew as large as houses.
My father who went to Judgment Day—
In this way, ah, God came to his aid.
All the saints gathered together.
Where they stood saying the funeral prayer,
Red willows grew in profusion.
The holy elders whose shrine it became—
Thus they had taken possession of it all.
All its signs could be seen;
Everything had become clear.
Seeing this, Semetey—
The orphan wept long in his distress,
Weeping, “My formidable father!”
The orphan sobbed and wept long,
Weeping, “My protector, my father!”
When he looked to his right,
There, when my formidable father died,
My noble mother Kanykei,
When she was left in mourning,
Cried out, “My bloodthirsty one!”
My noble mother sobbed:
“I shall plunge a knife into my belly.
How can I remain after my bloodthirsty one?”
My noble mother Kanykei—
That was where she stood helpless,
Her precious hair that no comb had touched—
That was where she tore it out strand by strand.
Then at Ken-Shor
Groves and willows sprang up in stands.
For my father who went to the next world,
Thus the Creator came to his aid.
The traces of my mother Kanykei—
The orphan longs to see them.
Sobbing, “My leopard father!”
At times he longs to die.
Ah, my poor mother, whom I cherish!
The dark tears flowing from her eyes
There at Ken-Shor
Became pools of spring water.
My khan father, whom I cherish,
Had been a banner to the people.
Her ruddy face, like a plane tree—
That was where my mother screamed and clawed it.
The dark blood from my mother's face
Became red stone where it fell.
My father had been the people's head.
When my khan father Manas died,
When the people gathered and buried him,
When my noble mother Kanykei
Suffered every torment,
Eleman's warrior Toshtuk,
Eshtektei's Zhamgyrchy,
Khan Tekechi and Khan Shygai,
All the Muslims wailed.
Bakai and Koshoi the Lion wept.
All the saints wept for my khan father.
The multitude wept; the people wept.
All the many peoples wept for my khan father.
Ezhigei and Shyiyk both wept.
Aikozho of Andizhan wept apart.
Many kinds of lion warriors wept.
“We are like a fire gone out,” they said.
Argyns and Kyrgyz wept together.
Without letting anyone know,
Without anyone becoming aware,
Taking a man's role though a woman,
My poor mother, whom I cherish,
Making a banner of her mourning self,
Fearing treachery among the Argyns:
“If I bury my matchless, fierce-maned hero
In a place that is known,
They will all be my ruin.
All who bear a grudge
May take their revenge on the dead.
Will they open his grave?
Will they inflict torment openly?
Dragging him out onto the road,
Will they tear my lord apart for the dogs?
If the enemy should run wild,
Will they take revenge like this?
Will they dig a pit for me?
Will they make my misery boil?
Abyke and Kobosh, the six wicked ones,
With their treacherous thoughts,
Share a father with the Magnanimous One.
They themselves are the younger wife's sons.
Deception lurks in their eyes.
If they can, they seek to trip me up.
Guile lies in their eyes.
Mischief lurks in their words.
This Talas is no land for us.
These Kyrgyz are no people for us.”
My mother pondered this,
Spent her wealth,
And had the face of the earth searched.
From the lower city of Mekedyl
She had eighty strongmen brought.
Taking care of my father,
She concealed the Magnanimous One's remains.
Except for magnanimous Bakai,
No one looking can find it;
Its whereabouts are unknown.
“My uncle Bakai, bringer of good fortune—
The inheritance left by my father
I shall find at last.
I shall see the place where he was buried.
Before my fierce-maned father
I shall make my pilgrimage.”
Traveling on from there,
Of his father, Sultan Manas,
Every trace appeared.
Unable to contain his lament,
The orphan bereft of his father
Shed tears from his eyes.
The golden-bladed battle-ax
He pressed to his side, sobbing.
“Never having seen my leopard father's face,
Where is anyone as wretched as I?” he said.
The sole hero left by Manas
Sobbed and shed tears.
Along the lower reaches of the Talas,
In the hollow of Zhylgynduu,
At Kainar's dark springhead,
Beside the lone plane tree itself,
Opposite Bar-Kol,
In the garden King Manas planted,
Below Tort-Kul—
“My mother told me:
‘Your lion father's great mosque,
Where he said the prayers of Islam,
Is there,’ she said.
Let me reach that mosque.
At the legacy left by my father Manas
Let me recite the Qur'an.
To that place where my dear father walked,
I, an orphan with my grief,
Let me make a pilgrimage.”
To the ridge where the mosque stood
The orphan hero came.
The deeds of the six wicked ones
The boy Semetey saw.
When my magnanimous father died,
The vast wealth left by magnanimous Manas,
When they measured out shares with a whip,
When they plundered Khan Manas's possessions,
When they wreaked their mischief,
When they did as they pleased,
My unfortunate mother in mourning—
When they beat and struck her with whips,
When they devised their evil scheme,
My poor, fierce mother—
When they slashed her breasts,
Treating my mother like the carcass in kok-boru,
Putting her across a horse,
When they dragged her up and down,
When they brought down terrible calamity,
When they contrived their scheme,
All the fat of her buttocks,
When they slashed it with whips,
Blood flowed from her buttocks.
My poor, ill-fated mother—
Her child was young; her strength failed.
When they scattered the treasury,
Finding nowhere to seek support,
My leopard mother fled.
Putting all her thoughts to wisdom,
She escaped with him alive,
The child left by magnanimous Manas.
Taking possession of great wealth,
Abyke and Kobosh became mighty men in Talas.
Their noses bulging like leather bottles,
Brutish and running wild,
The wicked ones swaggered like slaves whose master had died.
Climbing a hill, they shouted,
Raising Kobosh as their battle cry.
